title: már + Past Tense: Marking an Experience as Having Happened

sections.title: A new kind of past-tense sentence
sections.content: Until now you've used past tense to narrate a specific event in a story: *Tegnap moziba mentem* ("Yesterday I went to the cinema") — one thing, one time, one place in a sequence. *már* opens a different door: it turns the same past-tense verb into a statement about your whole life so far — that this thing has happened to you at least once, without saying exactly when. *Voltam Londonban* and *Már voltam Londonban* are both past tense; *már* makes it explicit that you mean your experience so far ("have you ever been?") rather than telling a specific story.

sections.title: Same verb, different job
rows: Yesterday I was in London. (one specific trip)
I've already been to London. (an experience I have)
I've already eaten caviar. (at some point in my life)

items.english: Have you ever been to Japan?

items.spanish: Igen, már jártam Japánban, kétszer is.
items.english: Yes, I've already been to Japan, twice even.

sections.content: *már* usually stands next to the verb: right after it in a question (*Jártál már Japánban?*), in front of it in a statement (*Már jártam Japánban.*). More important than word order: *már* signals "at some point up to now", so don't add a specific time word like *tegnap* or *2019-ben* in the same sentence — that turns it into a story about one occasion instead of a statement about your experience.
